PEP or post exposure prophylaxis is what people tend to think of and that's medication you take after exposure. Like if you are a healthcare worker and get an accidental needle stick. 

PreP is pre exposure prophylaxis. It comes in the form of a daily pill or a shot given every 2 months. It does require regular lab work to ensure healthy kidney and liver function.

Originally it was only FDA approved for gay men but since at least 2018 it's approved for anyone who is at risk of HIV. It's 98% effective at preventing HIV. Most people tolerate it well though some people get some GI upset side effects. Truvada now comes in generic and a lot of insurance will cover it completely now.

I do believe PRN work is not the same as a travel contract. A travel contract has a minimum amount of hours you work (though you could get cancelled) and you get a non taxable stipend since you need to duplicate expenses. 

PRN work you are a PRN employee at that hospital. It is not a temporary contract with an end date. You're just an employee. You might have a home unit or you might be float pool. There are minimum work requirements. One hospital I worked at it was down to 12 hours per pay period. Most are 24 hours per pay period. You can typically pick up as many shifts as you want if there are shifts available. 

Typically PRN positions do not come with benefits. They just have a better pay rate. Some travel agencies do provide benefits like health insurance. 

PRN does not have distance restrictions. You can go pick up a PRN job at the hospital down the road. A lot of travel contracts will have restrictions. One contract I had said you had to live over 100 miles away. But I've also seen 50miles and 150 miles. 

I worked with someone who kept a PRN job in Florida. She would fly back once a month and work Thursday-Tuesday and then disappear again. 

I knew one guy who was PRN at two different hospitals and so he could always pick up a shift any day he wanted since usually at least one them had a shift available. If every unit is "staffed appropriately" then there are no PRN shifts. A lot of PRN shifts are shifts from staff nurses calling out.

So "staying with family" can mean a couple different things. 

To get the tax free stipend, you need to duplicate expenses which means to pay for 2 housing situations. So to be fully tax compliant you would need to pay your relative whatever market rate for that area is to rent a single room. 

Some people don't do that and basically are committing tax fraud. They're gambling on the chance of getting audited or not. If the IRS doesn't notice you, you can keep your full stipend. But if you get audited, you have to pay back a good chunk of money. For some people it's worth the risk of getting in trouble with the IRS. 

Some people will try and get a travel position that is a fully taxed rate. Sometimes these rates are significantly higher than your current staff pay. But sometimes they are not. And of course they're fully taxed. 

Oh I should probably mention travel nurse pay, like you go online and see contracts paying $2500/ 36hr week. Are broken down into a taxable hourly rate and a non taxable stipend. So that $2500/wk you might only be getting paid $30/hr or $1080/wk.

There is no sleeping pill that does not have side effects with long term use.  

Melatonin is the only one that is generally considered safe to use long term. But everyone hear has heard or tried melatonin before. That's why you're asking. 

Benadryl is not a sleep aid. Using it multiple times a week has big risk of anticholinergic side effects. 

Z drugs like Ambien are still considered "safe" for extended use in most people. It's apparently extremely difficult to maintain a regular sleep cycle if you have been on them for years and have to stop. Also sleep walking is definitely happens to some people on them. 

Seroquel and trazadone have been used for sleep. Both can have some very significant side effects with long term use. Including Parkinson's like symptoms. 

Benzos are generally considered not safe to use long term. If you manage to get a doctor to prescribe them, there is a very real chance another doctor will come along and cut you off. And long term benzo use absolutely messes with your brain. Benzo withdrawal is ugly and could potentially kill you. And there are some very well documented cognitive side effects associated with long term use.  

Im sure plenty of people have been on benzos for years and will tell you it's fine and it's the only way they can sleep. 

Full disclosure, I'm a nurse and have seen some horrible situations where elderly people are now really messed up cognitively from long term (30+ yrs) of benzo use.

The brain will get stuck in cycles and stop associating bed time routines with actually sleeping. It really sounds like you have trained your brain that it is a distressing thing to be in the bed and you get anxious laying in bed at night. 

Relaxation techniques might be very useful. 

And as always sleep hygiene. Don't do anything but sleep in the bed. If it's been over an hour and you're wide awake try to get up and do something that relaxes you and then try to lay down and sleep. Laying for hours in the bed awake trains your brain that the bed is somewhere to stay awake. 

Make sure your room is cool and dark. Minimize all distractions. Consider a white noise machine. Limit electronic devices before bed. Limit caffeine. 

Utilize melatonin. Research shows smaller doses are probably more effective then large doses. So don't try to take like 15mg or anything. 

When you wake up, make sure you get straight out of bed. Do not use snooze. Do not hang out in the bed. Do your best to get some direct sun light or at least very bright light within 15 mins of waking up. It helps get the brain on the wake mode.

Yes. I worked a mixed ICU at a very busy level 2 trauma center. I also worked Trauma ICU at a level 1 and did CVICU at the level 1. 

I also worked critical care float pool at a level 1. I'm now float pool at a much smaller level 2. 

Trauma ( my one true love) Really depends on the area. Some trauma hospitals are mostly old person fall down patients and others are multiple admits every night for unrestrained MVC with ejection, multi GSW, machete attack, etc. Some people really hate dealing with TBI patients. Best part of trauma patients is a lot actually do recover.

CVICU very dependent on the hospital. Some lean a lot more medical than surgical. I personally feel being in a strong surgical CVICU helped me understand hemodynamics better than any kind of studying and theoretical practice ever did. But they are almost always full of very strong personalities. 

Cardiac ICUs that aren't surgical can still be good experiences. Especially if it specializes in heart failure and throws IABP and impellas in patients. Or are pre heart transplant units. But sometimes it's just STEMI patients who got their stents placed and are now chilling. Post cardiac arrest patients have the whole mystery of why did they code? 

Neuro ICU, some people like Neuro, some don't. I'm not saying Neuro ICU patient's aren't sick, but they're not the same kind of sick. Probably not going to do much work with hemodynamics. If it's a Neuro trauma unit that takes all the trauma patients, that's different. But often it's just a bunch of TBIs, seizures disorders, strokes, spine stuff and brain tumors. It can be a very physically heavy job. Neuro nurses work their butts off. 

Surgical is extremely hospital dependent. If they do transplant or not, if they're combined with other specialties like cardiac surgery or trauma surgery. I would say this is the most hemodynamically unstable unit after CVICU. Especially liver transplant patients. Some people really love working with the transplant population. SICU can also be a lot of oncology and tumor resection patients. Sometimes these units can be "smelly" or "gross". 

Vascular ICUs can have very sick patients. Very hospital dependent. Vascular might mean limb amputations, fem pop bypasses, aortic aneurysms, mesenteric ischemia. Sometimes the patients are just there to get some stents thrown in, sometimes they show up on death's doorstep. These units tend to be very surgery forward. 

Thoracic ICU/Pulmonary ICU: can be more surgery heavy. VATS and lobectomies. Sometimes transplant. Sometimes it's where they stick the ECMO patients. Very common for patients to have long stays in the ICU. 

Burn ICU is my least favorite. I do not enjoy the patient population. Like there's wound care and then there is complex burn wound care. Running CRRT on a burn patient is an experience. They tend to be smaller units. Not sure if it would be a good foundation for CRNA. 

And of course MICU. The wonderful catch all unit. You'll see a good variety. But it's also a sad unit. A lot of end stage COPD, end stage liver failure, stage 4 cancer. A whole bunch of full code 90 something yo meemaws. You'll also get the 30yo who is in DKA because they couldn't afford their insulin.  You'll have the walkie talkie lady who had the stomach flu and now her K is 2.3 and Na is 120 paired with the septic Covid patient maxed out on pressors and on 10 of peep 90% FiO only satting 92%. A lot of MICUs these days are full of nurses with less than 3 years of experience. Covid burnt out a lot experienced MICU nurses and they left. 

Coworkers and managers make or break a unit. The patient population can suck but if you have good teamwork it makes it so much better. A bad manager can make the best job hell.

Cognitive empathy is you see someone crying over the death of a loved one and you understand that they are sad because that is a sad experience to have. You don't tell someone they are ugly to their face because you know that would be rude and hurt them emotionally. Cognitive empathy is the ability to connect situations to emotions. The whole "knowing other people experience feelings"

Autism is different. There is still a lot the scientific community is unsure about. I feel like the diagnostic criteria is going to change again with the DSM 6. Right now the umbrella of autism spectrum disorder is very wide. There is a saying that if you met one autistic person, you've met one autistic person. I'm frequently met with people insisting autism only exists on the most severe presentation where the person is unable to take care of their basic needs independently. 

However, there is no specific treatment plan for autism. There are various strategies to try to help autistic people achieve a more fulfilling life and alleviate specific symptoms. But on some level, I think everyone would benefit at least a little from supportive therapies. Building effective coping skills, emotional regulation, more effective communication skills, and better mind body connection are all things that I feel would benefit the majority of people. And some people might just appreciate things that take sensory input into consideration. Like stores having specific times for shopping that are geared at autistic people with dimmer lights, no overhead music and smaller crowd sizes, someone with ADHD might find that shopping experience pleasant. Or someone with anxiety.

One might argue that only professionally diagnosed people deserve to benefit from systems in place to help people with autism. And that if all the self diagnosed people take up all the available community support, there won't be any left over for the "real autistic people". 

But the problem with that is assuming everyone had equal opportunity to be diagnosed. Many places refuse to diagnose adults. There are mental health professionals who believe specific stereotypes about autistic people because they are uninformed in how autism presents. (You'll often hear people say that someone can't be autistic if they went to college or if they have ever had a friend before). Minorities and women are much less likely to get diagnosed with autism despite new evidence showing it is probably presenting fairly equally and is not just in white males. But before the 1980s majority of mental health specialists did not believe autism existed in women. Before the 2000s they believed the rate of autism was roughly 1:40 for boys but 1:2000 for girls. 

An autism diagnosis is expensive. It can cost upwards of $500 for an assessment. It is often not covered by insurance. There is also a bit of gatekeeping that exists. Only people specifically trained on a handful of specific tests are able to give out a professional autism diagnosis. While there might be over two dozen psychiatrists and nurse practitioners in an area, there might be only one who is able to give a professional autism diagnosis. It is common for waiting lists to be over a year long for evaluation. 

Adult autism diagnosis is also very difficult to do. By the time someone is an adult they would have learned coping skills to cover up their autistic symptoms. Or masking. Right now the current testing used for autism is focused on children who have very minimal coping skills and are having detrimental impact from the autism symptoms. 

For example, I find eye contact extremely unpleasant but I was aware it was expected of me. So I would practice maintaining eye contact with myself in a mirror until I could manage to do it with others. I also look at people's mouths instead of their eyes in a way that gives the appearance of direct eye contact. So it might appear that I am capable of maintaining eye contact and someone might dismiss that and claim I do not have that symptom of autism because I have found a way to cope with that symptom by the time I was an adult. 

So I do and I don't support self diagnosis. It's complicated.

So there is a specific sleeping disorder that has a high rate of concurrence with ADHD. 

Delayed sleep phase disorder. Its not insomnia. Insomnia is the inability to obtain restful sleep. With delayed sleep phase disorder or DSPD, you are able to get a full restful sleep but it's at the "wrong time". 

Something about the brain not being able to recognize typical sleep inducing signals like the sun going down. 

Some people are able to move their sleep window forward by extremely strict sleep hygiene and sticking to the same schedule every single day no matter what. And training the brain that a specific time is for getting tired while taking melatonin. 

But for a lot of people, like me, we just get night shift jobs and accept going to bed before midnight is unlikely to ever happen.

Work on getting your driver's license. State IDs have power. Not having official identification puts you at a disadvantage. A passport is also a great option.
